extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, philosophy, and semantics (general readers of a logical treatise)
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical/logical treatment that defines and classifies types of names (relative, univocal, equivocal, analogical) and enumerates the kinds of things names can denote (feelings, substances, attributes), with guidance on usage and common confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of relative names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is said to be relative, when, over and above the object which it denotes, it implies in its signification the existence of another object, also deriving a denomination from the same fact which is the ground of the first name. (Or: a name is relative when, being the name of one thing, its signification cannot be explained but by mentioning another.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative names cannot be employed in discourse so as to have meaning unless the name of some other thing is either expressed or understood. Example: 'father' connotes the fact as an attribute of A; 'son' connotes the same fact as an attribute of B. If all other objects were annihilated, attributes expressed by relative names would be swept away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal vs equivocal (sequivocal) application of names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is univocal, or applied univocally, with respect to all things of which it can be predicated in the same sense; but it is equivocally (sequi-vocally) applied as respects those things of which it is predicated in different senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous words are effectively two (or more) distinct names that coincide in sound; treating them as one word is misleading. Examples: 'file' (tool) vs 'file' (line of soldiers); 'grease' vs 'Greece'. Recognize accidental coincidence of sound rather than unity of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical or metaphorical use of names and its fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A name used analogically or metaphorically is predicated of two things not univocally but in somewhat similar significations, one derived from the other (primary and secondary meanings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'brilliant' in 'brilliant light' vs 'brilliant achievement'. The word is in effect two names; a common fallacy is to argue from a metaphorical expression as if it were literal — treating a transferred meaning as identical with the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation of relative names includes actions, contingencies, and third-party remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Many relative names connote not only a relation but also a body of actions (past, present, possible/future) associated with the bearers of the names, and sometimes actions by others under contingencies (e.g., legal enforcement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'sovereign' and 'subject' connote reciprocal actions; 'physician' and 'patient'; legal relations like 'mortgagor'/'mortgagee' connote what a court would do to enforce obligations. When assessing the meaning of such names, include these connoted actions and contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action analyzed as volition plus effect
rubrics_metrics.description: An action is a compound: the volition or intention to produce an effect (a state of mind) followed by the effect produced (a physical fact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: intending to move my arm (volition) and the arm moving (effect) together constitute the action. This analysis is used to account for how actions are included in the connotation of names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerating what names can denote (basis for predication)
rubrics_metrics.description: To know what can be predicated or be the subject of affirmation/denial, we must enumerate the kinds of things signified by names: the principal classes identified are Feelings (states of consciousness), Substances, and Attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy is presented as the foundation for understanding propositions and predicates; the subsequent subdivisions refine what is meant by each class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of feelings (states of consciousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings (states of consciousness) form a genus whose species are Sensations, Emotions, Thoughts, and Volitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoughts are the mind's internal states (ideas, beliefs), distinct from external objects; sensations must be distinguished from the object causing them and from attributes named for that sensation. Volitions are will-acts and figure in the connotation of many relational names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sensation, bodily-organ state, perception, and belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensation is a state of the sentient mind; the bodily-organ state (retina, nerve, brain phenomena) is a distinct physical fact not directly conscious; perception (recognition of an external cause) is sometimes treated as a separate act of mind and amounts to an intuitive belief that an external cause exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophically, sensations are mental, bodily states are physical, and 'perception' as belief belongs to metaphysics rather than logic. For logical analysis, treat perceptions as kinds of belief (states of mind) but recognize their different epistemic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language limitations: single words often conflate sensation, attribute, and object
rubrics_metrics.description: Common language often lacks single-word designations for sensations, so words like 'colour' stand indifferently for (a) the sensation, (b) the attribute (whiteness), and (c) the object property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of this conflation: it causes confusion in analysis (e.g., distinguishing sensation of white vs whiteness vs white object). When precision is required, use circumlocution ('the sensation of whiteness') or careful qualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Aristotelian Categories (requirements for a useful classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional list of categories (substance, quantity, quality, relation, action, passion, where, when, position, habit) is defective and redundant: it omits important items (feelings, states of mind), repeats others under different heads, and misplaces distinctions like action/passivity and time/space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory classification should avoid redundancy, include feelings/states of consciousness as first-class items, and seek analytic rationale rather than mere cataloguing from ordinary language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance versus attribute: linguistic test and metaphysical caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Common logician test: an attribute must be the attribute 'of' something (requires an 'of'), whereas a substance can be conceived as self-existent (not 'of' something).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This linguistic test is useful but insufficient: it pushes the explanatory burden onto the particle 'of' and ignores that both substances and attributes may be conceived in isolation. Metaphysicians further distinguish substances into Bodies and Minds for a more satisfactory account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Body as the external cause of sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: A Body (as a kind of substance) may be defined as the external cause to which we ascribe our sensations; the external something considered independent of mind and bodily organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as a way to characterize bodies for logical/metaphysical accounts, but the author notes there are metaphysical controversies about whether we are warranted in ascribing sensations to external causes; the definition is to be used as a practical stance for defending the existence of substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on using ambiguous or shifting terminology (Being/Entity/Essence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'Being', 'Being', 'Entity', and 'Essence' have ambiguous and shifting connotations: 'being' and 'being' tend to become synonymous with 'substance', and words originally meant to connote mere existence gradually take on implications of separate or independent existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer should (a) warn readers about these ambiguities, (b) choose for each occasion the word least likely to mislead, and (c) accept some flexible/improper use of terms when it helps convey meaning, while making an effort to avoid leaving meaning doubtful or obscure.
